questions.stem: The standard merge step combines the sorted runs `[2, 11, 17, 23, 29]` and `[6, 13, 18]`: compare the two front items, move the smaller one out, and stop comparing as soon as one run is empty. How many comparisons are made?

traps.why: Used the worst-case bound m + n - 1 = 7; the second run empties while 23 and 29 remain, and they are copied free.
Used the best-case bound min(m, n) = 3; the runs interleave, so more comparisons are needed.
Counted one comparison per output item; the leftover items are copied without comparing.

questions.solution:
1. 2<6, 6<11, 11<13, 13<17, 17<18, 18<23: 6 comparisons, output `[2, 6, 11, 13, 17, 18]`.
2. The second run is now empty, so 23 and 29 are copied with no comparison. Total 6.

questions.stem: Two sorted runs of sizes 5 and 7 are merged with the standard merge step (stop comparing when one run is empty). Over all possible inputs, what are the minimum and the maximum numbers of comparisons?

options.text: Minimum 5, maximum 11
options.why: Best case: the 5 smaller items leave after 5 comparisons. Worst case: interleaving until the end, 5 + 7 - 1 = 11.

options.text: Minimum 5, maximum 12
options.why: Counted m + n; the very last item is copied without a comparison because the other run is already empty.

options.text: Minimum 7, maximum 11
options.why: Used the larger run for the best case; the merge stops as soon as the shorter run (5 items) is used up.

options.text: Minimum 11, maximum 11
options.why: Assumed a merge always costs m + n - 1; it stops early when one run empties, so the cost depends on the data.

questions.solution:
1. Fewest: every item of the 5-run is smaller than the first item of the 7-run. Each comparison outputs one of them, so 5 comparisons, then the 7 items are copied.
2. Most: the runs interleave until only one item is left, so 12 - 1 = 11 items leave by comparison.
3. Range 5 to 11, i.e. min(m, n) to m + n - 1.

questions.stem: Top-down merge sort (`mid = n // 2`; sort the left half completely, then the right half, then merge them) runs on `[38, 12, 27, 5, 44, 19, 31, 8]`. Number the merges in the order they are executed. What is the output of merge number 4?

options.why: Merges 1-3 finish the left half ([12, 38], [5, 27], [5, 12, 27, 38]); the right half starts with 44 and 19, so merge 4 gives [19, 44].
This is the 4th merge of bottom-up merge sort, which does all size-1 merges first; top-down finishes the left half, including its size-2 merge, before the right half.
Off by one: this is merge 3, the last merge of the left half; merge 4 is the first merge inside the right half.
Recursed into the right part before the left at every level; with left first, [5, 27] is merge 2.

questions.solution:
1. Left half `[38, 12, 27, 5]`: merge 1 = [12, 38], merge 2 = [5, 27], merge 3 = [5, 12, 27, 38].
2. Right half `[44, 19, 31, 8]`: merge 4 = [19, 44], merge 5 = [8, 31], merge 6 = [8, 19, 31, 44].
3. Merge 7 produces the whole sorted array. Merge 4 outputs `[19, 44]`.

questions.stem: Top-down merge sort with `mid = n // 2` (so 7 keys split as 3 + 4, and 3 keys as 1 + 2) sorts `[32, 17, 26, 36, 8, 38, 48]`. Each merge stops comparing as soon as one run is empty. What is the total number of key comparisons over all merges?

traps.why: Used m + n - 1 for every merge (1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 6), the worst case; several merges stop early here.
Split 7 keys as 4 + 3 (mid = (n + 1) // 2); the question fixes mid = n // 2, giving 3 + 4.
Counted one comparison per merge; there are 6 merges, but most cost more than one comparison.

questions.stem: Which statements about top-down merge sort (standard merge that stops comparing when one run is empty) are true?

options.text: Sorting n ≥ 1 keys performs exactly n - 1 merge operations.
options.why: Start with n runs of size 1; each merge turns two runs into one, so n - 1 merges leave a single run.

options.text: For n = 32 keys, the maximum total number of comparisons is 129.
options.why: Worst case for n = 2^k is n log₂ n - n + 1 = 32·5 - 32 + 1 = 129.

options.text: On an already sorted array of 16 keys it makes only 15 comparisons, one per merge.
options.why: In each merge the left run empties first and costs its full length: 8 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 32 comparisons.

options.text: Merging two runs of 8 keys each always takes exactly 15 comparisons.
options.why: 15 is only the worst case; if one run's keys are all smaller it empties after 8 comparisons.

questions.solution:
1. n runs of size 1 become one run, and each merge reduces the number of runs by one: n - 1 merges.
2. Worst case for n = 2^k: n log₂ n - n + 1; for n = 32 that is 160 - 32 + 1 = 129.
3. Sorted input, 16 keys: every merge costs the length of its left run: 8·1 + 4·2 + 2·4 + 1·8 = 32, not 15.
4. Two runs of 8 cost anywhere from 8 to 15 comparisons, depending on the keys.

questions.stem: Bottom-up merge sort runs on 20 keys: pass 1 merges adjacent runs of size 1, pass 2 runs of size 2, and so on; an unpaired last run is carried unchanged to the next pass. How many passes are needed until one sorted run remains?

options.why: Runs go 20 → 10 → 5 → 3 → 2 → 1, so 5 passes (⌈log₂ 20⌉ = 5).
Used ⌊log₂ 20⌋ = 4; after 4 passes runs of 16 and 4 keys are still separate.
Counted the merges of pass 1 (20 / 2 = 10), not the passes.
19 = n - 1 is the total number of merge operations over all passes, not the number of passes.

questions.solution:
1. Number of runs after each pass: 20 → 10 → 5 → 3 → 2 → 1.
2. That is 5 passes, i.e. ⌈log₂ 20⌉ = 5.

questions.stem:
`partition(a, 0, 7)` below (Lomuto) is called on `a = [21, 5, 34, 13, 8, 40, 2, 17]`. What index does it return?

```python
def partition(a, lo, hi):
    pivot = a[hi]
    i = lo - 1
    for j in range(lo, hi):
        if a[j] <= pivot:
            i += 1
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    a[i + 1], a[hi] = a[hi], a[i + 1]
    return i + 1
```

traps.why: Gave the 1-based position of the pivot (or counted the pivot itself); indices here are 0-based.
Returned the last value of i; the pivot goes to i + 1.
Gave the pivot's starting index hi; partition moves it to its sorted place.

questions.solution:
1. Pivot = a[7] = 17. Among a[0..6] the keys ≤ 17 are 5, 13, 8, 2, so i moves from -1 to 3.
2. The final swap puts 17 at i + 1 = 4: a = `[5, 13, 8, 2, 17, 40, 21, 34]`, and 4 is returned.

questions.stem:
Quicksort below (Lomuto `partition`, left part first) runs as `quicksort(a, 0, 7)` on `a = [14, 3, 10, 18, 6, 1, 12, 8]`. What is `a` right after the **second** call to `partition` returns?

```python
def partition(a, lo, hi):
    pivot = a[hi]
    i = lo - 1
    for j in range(lo, hi):
        if a[j] <= pivot:
            i += 1
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    a[i + 1], a[hi] = a[hi], a[i + 1]
    return i + 1
```

```python
def quicksort(a, lo, hi):
    if lo < hi:
        p = partition(a, lo, hi)
        quicksort(a, lo, p - 1)
        quicksort(a, p + 1, hi)
```

options.why: Call 1 gives [3, 6, 1, 8, 14, 10, 12, 18]; call 2 on a[0..2] has pivot 1, nothing is ≤ 1, so 1 swaps with 3.
This is the array after the first call only.
This is after the third call (on a[1..2]); the second call only places pivot 1.
Assumed keys larger than the pivot keep their original order; Lomuto's swaps leave 14, 10, 12 and send 18 to the end.

questions.solution:
1. Call 1, pivot 8: the keys ≤ 8 (3, 6, 1) are swapped to the front, then 8 goes to index 3: a = `[3, 6, 1, 8, 14, 10, 12, 18]`, p = 3.
2. Call 2 is `partition(a, 0, 2)` on [3, 6, 1], pivot 1: no key is ≤ 1, so 1 swaps with a[0].
3. a = `[1, 6, 3, 8, 14, 10, 12, 18]`.

questions.stem:
Quicksort below (Lomuto `partition`, pivot = last element) sorts `[6, 13, 2, 9, 4, 11, 7]` via `quicksort(a, 0, 6)`. How many comparisons `a[j] <= pivot` are made in total?

```python
def partition(a, lo, hi):
    pivot = a[hi]
    i = lo - 1
    for j in range(lo, hi):
        if a[j] <= pivot:
            i += 1
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    a[i + 1], a[hi] = a[hi], a[i + 1]
    return i + 1
```

```python
def quicksort(a, lo, hi):
    if lo < hi:
        p = partition(a, lo, hi)
        quicksort(a, lo, p - 1)
        quicksort(a, p + 1, hi)
```

traps.why: Used the worst case n(n - 1)/2 = 21; this input splits fairly evenly.
Counted k comparisons for a part of k keys (7 + 3 + 3 + 2); the pivot is not compared with itself.
Counted the swaps executed (9) instead of the comparisons.

questions.solution:
1. partition(0, 6), pivot 7: 6 comparisons; a = [6, 2, 4, 7, 13, 11, 9], p = 3.
2. Left [6, 2, 4], pivot 4: 2 comparisons → [2, 4, 6], p = 1; both sides have one key, no more calls.
3. Right [13, 11, 9], pivot 9: 2 comparisons → [9, 11, 13], p = 4; then [11, 13], pivot 13: 1 comparison.
4. Total 6 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 11.

questions.stem: Which statements about quicksort with the Lomuto `partition` (pivot = a[hi], test `a[j] <= pivot`) are true?

options.text: It is not stable: on `[2a, 2b, 1]` (2a and 2b are equal keys) it outputs `[1, 2b, 2a]`.
options.why: The first partition swaps pivot 1 with a[0] = 2a, sending 2a behind 2b; the second partition (pivot 2a) keeps 2b in front.

options.text: If the pivot is always the true median (found in linear time), the worst case becomes Θ(n log n).
options.why: Every split is n/2 : n/2 with Θ(n) work, so T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) = Θ(n log n) on every input.

options.text: Partitioning 10 keys makes 10 comparisons.
options.why: The pivot is not compared with itself: j runs over the other 9 keys, so 9 comparisons.

options.text: Choosing the pivot uniformly at random makes the worst-case time Θ(n log n).
options.why: Random pivots give Θ(n log n) expected time; an unlucky run of pivots can still cost Θ(n²).

questions.solution:
1. `[2a, 2b, 1]` (2a, 2b equal keys): pivot 1, nothing ≤ 1, swap a[0] ↔ a[2] → [1, 2b, 2a]; the next partition keeps 2b first. Not stable.
2. A median pivot splits n/2 : n/2, so T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) = Θ(n log n) in the worst case.
3. The loop runs j = lo .. hi - 1: 9 comparisons for 10 keys.
4. A random pivot gives Θ(n log n) expected time only; the worst case stays Θ(n²).

questions.stem: Lomuto `partition(a, lo, hi)` (pivot = a[hi], test `a[j] <= pivot`) returns p. Which statement always holds right after it returns?

options.text: Every key in a[lo..p-1] is ≤ a[p], and every key in a[p+1..hi] is > a[p].
options.why: Keys passing the ≤ test are moved to the front, the rest stay behind, and the pivot is placed between them.

options.text: Every key in a[lo..p-1] is < a[p], and every key in a[p+1..hi] is ≥ a[p].
options.why: The test is <=, so keys equal to the pivot go to the left part, not the right.

options.text: Both a[lo..p-1] and a[p+1..hi] are sorted.
options.why: Partition only separates small keys from large ones; each side is still unsorted, which is why quicksort recurses on it.

options.text: p = (lo + hi) // 2, the middle index.
options.why: p is lo plus the number of keys ≤ the pivot; it is the middle only when the pivot happens to be the median.

questions.solution:
1. Keys passing `a[j] <= pivot` are swapped into the front block a[lo..i]; the others stay behind it.
2. The pivot is swapped to i + 1 = p, so the left part holds keys ≤ pivot and the right part keys > pivot.
3. Neither part is sorted, and p depends on the data, not on the middle index.

questions.stem: Solve $T(n) = 2T(n/4) + \sqrt{n}$.

options.text: $\Theta(\sqrt{n}\,\log n)$
options.why: $n^{\log_4 2} = \sqrt{n}$ equals f(n), so each of the $\log_4 n$ levels costs $\Theta(\sqrt n)$.

options.text: $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$
options.why: Treated the equal case like case 3; when f matches $n^{\log_b a}$ one extra log factor appears.

options.text: $\Theta(n^2)$
options.why: Computed $\log_a b = \log_2 4 = 2$ instead of $\log_b a = \log_4 2 = 1/2$.

options.text: $\Theta(n \log n)$
options.why: Matched the merge-sort shape 2T(·) + f; here the subproblems are n/4 and f is $\sqrt n$, not n.

questions.solution:
1. a = 2, b = 4: $n^{\log_4 2} = n^{1/2}$, since $4^{1/2} = 2$.
2. $f(n) = \sqrt{n}$ equals $n^{\log_b a}$: the equal case, every level costs about $\sqrt{n}$.
3. There are $\log_4 n$ levels, so $T(n) = \Theta(\sqrt{n}\,\log n)$.

questions.stem: Solve $T(n) = 7T(n/3) + n^2$.

options.text: $\Theta(n^2)$
options.why: $\log_3 7 \approx 1.77 < 2$, so f(n) dominates (case 3) and $7(n/3)^2 = (7/9)n^2$ satisfies regularity.

options.text: $\Theta(n^{\log_3 7})$
options.why: Took the leaf term, but $n^2$ is polynomially larger than $n^{1.77}$, so the root level dominates.

options.text: $\Theta(n^2 \log n)$
options.why: Treated it as the equal case; $\log_3 7 \approx 1.77$ is not 2.
Used a/b = 7/3 as the exponent; the leaf exponent is $\log_b a$.

questions.solution:
1. $n^{\log_3 7}$ with $\log_3 7 \approx 1.77$ (since $3^{1.77} \approx 7$).
2. $f(n) = n^2$ is polynomially larger ($2 > 1.77$): case 3.
3. Regularity: $7(n/3)^2 = \tfrac{7}{9}n^2 \le c\,n^2$ with $c = 7/9 < 1$. So $T(n) = \Theta(n^2)$.

questions.stem:
What is the value of `count` after `h(16)` runs (with `count = 0` at the start)?

```python
count = 0
def h(n):
    global count
    if n <= 1:
        return
    for i in range(n):
        count += 1
    h(n // 2)
    h(n // 2)
    h(n // 2)
```

traps.why: Used two recursive calls per level (16 + 16 + 16 + 16); the code makes three.
Counted only the leaves 3^4 = 81; the leaves add nothing and the inner levels do all the counting.
Counted the number of calls 1 + 3 + 9 + 27 + 81 = 121, not the loop iterations.
Added 1 for each of the 81 base calls; the loop never runs when n ≤ 1.

questions.solution:
1. The code follows $T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n$ with nothing added for n ≤ 1.
2. Level i has $3^i$ calls of size $16/2^i$: sizes 16, 8, 4, 2 add 16, 3·8 = 24, 9·4 = 36, 27·2 = 54.
3. The 81 calls with n = 1 add nothing. Total 16 + 24 + 36 + 54 = 130.

questions.stem: Which recurrences (with $T(1) = 1$) have solution $T(n) = \Theta(n)$?

options.why: Work shrinks geometrically: n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n, so Θ(n) (case 3 with a = 1).
$n^{\log_2 2} = n$ is polynomially larger than f(n) = 1, so the leaves dominate: Θ(n).
Looks like the previous one, but two calls on n − 1 double at every step: $T(n) = 2^n - 1 = \Theta(2^n)$.
f(n) = n equals $n^{\log_2 2}$: the equal case gives Θ(n log n).

questions.solution:
1. $T(n/2) + n$: $n + n/2 + n/4 + \dots < 2n$, so $\Theta(n)$.
2. $2T(n/2) + 1$: $n^{\log_2 2} = n$ dominates f = 1, so $\Theta(n)$.
3. $2T(n-1) + 1$: unrolling gives $2^n - 1$, so $\Theta(2^n)$.
4. $2T(n/2) + n$: equal case, $\Theta(n \log n)$.

questions.stem: $T(n) = T(n/2) + n$ for $n > 1$ and $T(1) = 1$, where n is a power of 2. What is the exact value of $T(64)$?

traps.why: Stopped at the n = 2 term and dropped T(1) = 1.
Used the bound 2n; the exact sum is 2n − 1.
Treated it like merge sort, n log₂ n = 64·6; there is only one recursive call.

questions.stem: On the undirected graph shown, an iterative DFS starts with only A on a stack. It repeats: pop a vertex; if it is already visited, skip it; otherwise visit it and push all its unvisited neighbours **in alphabetical order**. In what order are the vertices visited?

options.text: A E F G H D C B
options.why: Pushing in alphabetical order makes the largest name pop first; after D the top is the C pushed by D, then B.

options.text: A B C D H G F E
options.why: This is the recursive DFS order with alphabetical neighbours; a stack that pushes A–Z pops them Z–A.

options.text: A B E C F G D H
options.why: This is the BFS order; a stack is LIFO, not FIFO.

options.text: A E F G H D B C
options.why: After D is visited the top of the stack is the C that D pushed, not one of the older B entries.

questions.solution:
1. Visit A, push B, E → [B, E]. Pop E, push F → [B, F]. Pop F, push B, G → [B, B, G].
2. Pop G, push B, C, H → [B, B, B, C, H]. Pop H, push D. Pop D, push C. Pop C, push B. Pop B.
3. The rest are skipped. Order A E F G H D C B.

questions.stem:
A directed graph is stored as adjacency lists, and BFS from vertex 0 scans each list **in the stored order**, marking a vertex when it is enqueued:

```python
adj = {0: [3, 1], 1: [4], 2: [0, 5], 3: [2, 4],
       4: [5, 6], 5: [1], 6: [], 7: [6]}
```

In what order are the vertices dequeued?

options.why: Level 1 is 3, 1 in stored order; 3 adds 2 and 4; 2 adds 5; 4 adds 6. Vertex 7 is not reachable.
Sorted each adjacency list; the question says to scan them in the stored order, so 3 comes before 1.
This is the DFS order (go deep along 0→3→2→5 first); BFS finishes level 1 before level 2.
The only edge at 7 is 7→6, which leaves 7; BFS from 0 follows arrows and never reaches 7.

questions.solution:
1. Dequeue 0: enqueue 3, 1. Dequeue 3: enqueue 2, 4. Dequeue 1: 4 is already marked.
2. Dequeue 2: 0 marked, enqueue 5. Dequeue 4: 5 marked, enqueue 6. Dequeue 5, then 6.
3. No edge enters 7, so it is never reached. Order 0 3 1 2 4 5 6.

4. Maximum 5.

questions.solution:
1. BFS from 1; paths(v) = sum of paths(u) over neighbours u one level up. paths(1) = 1.
2. Level 1: paths(2) = paths(5) = 1. Level 2: paths(3) = 1, paths(6) = 1 (only from 5), paths(9) = 1.
3. Level 3: paths(4) = 1, paths(7) = 1 + 1 = 2, paths(10) = 1 + 1 = 2. Level 4: paths(8) = 1 + 2 = 3, paths(11) = 2 (only from 10).
4. Level 5: paths(12) = paths(8) + paths(11) = 3 + 2 = 5.

questions.stem: BFS from s is run on a **directed** graph along edge directions, giving the level d(v) of every vertex v reachable from s. Which statements are always true?

options.text: For every edge u→v with u reachable from s, d(v) ≤ d(u) + 1.
options.why: When u is dequeued, v is already marked with a level ≤ d(u) + 1 or is given d(u) + 1.

options.text: For every edge u→v with u reachable from s, |d(u) − d(v)| ≤ 1.
options.why: That holds for undirected graphs; in s→a→b→s the edge b→s goes from level 2 down to level 0.

options.text: Every reachable v ≠ s with d(v) = k has an in-neighbour u with d(u) = k − 1.
options.why: v was enqueued while its BFS parent u at level k − 1 was scanned, and u→v is an edge.

options.text: If the graph is connected when directions are ignored, BFS from s reaches every vertex.
options.why: Directed BFS follows arrows only; with edges s→a and b→a, b is never reached from s.

questions.solution:
1. When u is dequeued, each out-neighbour v is either already marked (level ≤ d(u) + 1) or gets d(u) + 1.
2. The reverse bound fails: in s→a→b→s, edge b→s goes from level 2 to level 0.
3. A vertex at level k was enqueued from its BFS parent at level k − 1, which is an in-neighbour.
4. Directed BFS follows arrows only, so weak connectivity does not give reachability.

questions.stem: A DAG has edges a→b, a→d, b→c, d→c, c→e, d→f, f→e. Which sequence is **not** a valid topological order?

options.text: a d b f c e
options.why: Valid: every edge points forward. A DAG can have several topological orders.

options.text: a b d c f e
options.why: Valid: this is Kahn's order with alphabetical ties; b and d both precede c, and f precedes e.

options.text: a d f b c e
options.why: Valid: a child need not come right after its parent; only edge directions must be respected.

options.text: a b c d f e
options.why: c is placed before d, but the edge d→c requires d first.

questions.solution:
1. A topological order needs u before v for every edge u→v.
2. In a b c d f e, c comes before d, but d→c is an edge. So it is not valid.
3. The other three orders respect all seven edges.

questions.stem: A directed graph has edges p→q, p→s, q→r, r→p, r→t, s→t, t→u, u→s, v→u, v→w. DFS starts at p, scans out-neighbours in alphabetical order, and restarts from the alphabetically smallest unvisited vertex. One clock starts at 1 and increases by 1 at every discovery and every finish (so d[p] = 1). What is the finish time f[t]?

traps.why: Gave the discovery time d[t], not the finish time.
Gave t's rank in the finishing order (s, u, t); the clock also ticks at discoveries.
Scanned out-neighbours in reverse order, so p→s→t was taken first; the question fixes alphabetical order.

questions.solution:
1. d[p] = 1, d[q] = 2, d[r] = 3 (r→p: p is open), d[t] = 4, d[u] = 5, d[s] = 6.
2. s→t: t is open, so s finishes: f[s] = 7. Then f[u] = 8, f[t] = 9.
3. (Then f[r] = 10, f[q] = 11, f[p] = 12, and v, w get 13–16.)

questions.stem: A directed graph has edges a→b, a→d, a→e, b→c, b→d, c→a, d→c, e→d, f→b, f→e. DFS starts at a, scans out-neighbours in alphabetical order, and restarts from the alphabetically smallest unvisited vertex. Which statements are true?

options.text: a→d is a forward edge.
options.why: When a scans d (after b returns), d is finished and is a descendant of a: d[a] = 1 < d[d] = 5.

options.text: d→c is a back edge.
options.why: c finished (f = 4) before d was discovered (d = 5), so d→c is a cross edge; a back edge needs c still open.

options.text: c→a is a back edge, so the graph has a cycle.
options.why: a is still open (an ancestor of c) when c scans it; a→b→c→a is a cycle.

options.text: e→d is a tree edge.
options.why: d was discovered from b and finished before e was discovered (d[e] = 8), so e→d is a cross edge.

questions.solution:
1. Times (d/f): a 1/10, b 2/7, c 3/4, d 5/6, e 8/9, f 11/12.
2. c→a: a is open (an ancestor of c), so back edge; a→b→c→a is a cycle.
3. a→d: d finished, d[a] < d[d], so forward. d→c: c finished, d[c] < d[d], so cross.
4. e→d: d already finished before e was discovered, so cross, not tree.

options.text: s a c d b e
options.why: Took vertices in the order they were first reached (BFS-like); Dijkstra always extracts the smallest tentative distance, and c (1) beats a (3).

options.text: s c a b d e
options.why: Missed the relaxation c→d (1 + 3 = 4) and kept d[d] = 3 + 5 = 8, so b (5) seemed to come before d.

options.text: s c a d b e
options.why: Distances at extraction: s 0, c 1, a 3, d 4, b 5, e 8 — always the smallest unfinished value.

options.text: s c d e a b
options.why: Followed the cheapest edge out of the last vertex (a greedy walk s→c→d→e); Dijkstra compares total distances from s.

questions.solution:

2. Extract a (3): a→d gives 8 (no change), d[b] = 5. Extract d (4): d→b gives 10 (no change), d[e] = 9.
3. Extract b (5): d[e] = min(9, 8) = 8. Extract e. Order s c a d b e.

Took a path with the fewest edges (A–B–D–F or A–C–D–F); weights decide, not hop count.

questions.stem: A directed graph has edges s→a (2), s→b (7), a→d (3), b→a (−6), b→c (1). Dijkstra's algorithm (a vertex, once extracted, is never updated again) runs from s. For which vertices is the reported distance **different** from the true shortest distance?

options.text: a
options.why: a is finalized at 2 before b is extracted; the true distance via s→b→a is 7 − 6 = 1.

options.text: b
options.why: b is reached only by s→b (7), so 7 is correct; the negative edge leaves b, it does not enter it.

options.text: c
options.why: c's only route is s→b→c = 8, and d[b] is correct, so c is reported correctly.

options.text: d
options.why: d was finalized from the wrong d[a]: reported 2 + 3 = 5, true 1 + 3 = 4.

questions.solution:
1. Dijkstra: d[a] = 2, d[b] = 7; extract a (2): d[d] = 5; extract d (5); extract b (7): a is final, so b→a changes nothing; d[c] = 8.
2. True distances: a = min(2, 7 − 6) = 1, d = 1 + 3 = 4, b = 7, c = 8 (no cycle, so they are well defined).
3. Wrong for a (2 vs 1) and d (5 vs 4); correct for b and c.
